title: How disc brakes slow a bicycle
summary: Trace braking from caliper clamp force to rotor friction and understand why the rotor is fixed to the wheel.

steps.title: The rotor rotates with the wheel.
steps.body: The brake rotor is attached to the hub. Because it rotates with the wheel, slowing the rotor slows the wheel too.
steps.keyFact: A disc brake works on a rotor connected to the wheel, not directly on the tire.

steps.title: The caliper creates friction.
steps.body: Brake pads inside the caliper squeeze both sides of the rotating rotor. Friction converts the bicycle's kinetic energy primarily into heat.
steps.keyFact: The caliper stays with the frame or fork while the rotor moves through it.

steps.title: Braking is energy conversion.
steps.body: Hard or prolonged braking raises rotor and pad temperatures. Rotor size, airflow, pad material and braking technique affect thermal performance.
steps.keyFact: More braking power does not eliminate heat; it changes how quickly energy can be converted and managed.

steps.title: Find the rotating braking surface.
steps.body: Identify the part that turns with the wheel and passes through the stationary caliper.
steps.keyFact: The rotor is the moving friction surface.

challenge.prompt: Which part rotates through the brake caliper?
challenge.successText: Correct. The rotor is fixed to the hub and rotates through the caliper.
challenge.retryText: Not that one. Look for the thin circular braking surface attached to the wheel.
